content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed guidelines for the treatment of Neisseria gonorrhoeae infections, commonly known as gonorrhea. These guidelines address the growing challenge of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) and aim to provide evidence-based recommendations for the prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of gonococcal infections. Gonorrhea is the second most common bacterial sexually transmitted infection (STI) globally, causing significant morbidity and economic burden. It can present as urethritis in men and mucopurulent cervicitis in women, with rectal and pharyngeal infections often being asymptomatic. In women, asymptomatic infections can lead to severe complications such as pelvic inflammatory disease, ectopic pregnancy, and infertility. In men, untreated urethral infections may result in epididymitis, urethral strictures, and infertility. Neonates born to mothers with gonococcal infections are at risk of developing neonatal conjunctivitis, which can cause blindness if untreated. The diagnosis of N. gonorrhoeae can be made using culture, nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs), or Gram stain in symptomatic men. In settings without laboratory support, diagnosis is often based on clinical symptoms such as vaginal or urethral discharge. However, treatment is complicated by the rapidly evolving antimicrobial susceptibility patterns of N. gonorrhoeae, raising concerns about the emergence of untreatable infections with serious sexual and reproductive health consequences. Since the publication of the 2003 WHO guidelines for STI management, changes in the epidemiology of STIs and advancements in prevention, diagnosis, and treatment have necessitated updates to gonorrhea treatment protocols. High levels of resistance to previously recommended quinolones are now widespread, and decreased susceptibility to third-generation cephalosporins, another first-line treatment, has been reported in several countries. Treatment failures have also been documented. These developments underscore the urgent need for updated global treatment recommendations that account for local and global resistance patterns. The updated WHO guidelines recommend dual therapy as the preferred treatment for gonococcal infections, particularly in settings where local resistance data are unavailable. Dual therapy options include ceftriaxone (250 mg intramuscularly as a single dose) plus azithromycin (1 g orally as a single dose) or cefixime (400 mg orally as a single dose) plus azithromycin (1 g orally as a single dose). Single therapy may be considered only when reliable local resistance data confirm susceptibility to the chosen antimicrobial. For oropharyngeal gonococcal infections, dual therapy is also preferred due to observed treatment failures with single therapy. Pregnant women with gonococcal infections should be closely monitored for complications. In cases of treatment failure, the guidelines recommend re-treatment based on the suspected cause of failure. If reinfection is suspected, re-treatment with a WHO-recommended regimen, partner treatment, and reinforcement of safe sexual practices are advised. If failure occurs after treatment with a non-recommended regimen, re-treatment with a WHO-recommended regimen is suggested. For confirmed resistance, re-treatment should align with susceptibility data. If failure occurs after single therapy, dual therapy is recommended. For failures following dual therapy, alternative dual regimens, such as higher doses of ceftriaxone or cefixime combined with azithromycin, or gentamicin or spectinomycin combined with azithromycin, are suggested. For neonates with gonococcal conjunctivitis, treatment options include ceftriaxone (50 mg/kg intramuscularly, up to a maximum of 150 mg), kanamycin (25 mg/kg intramuscularly, up to a maximum of 75 mg), or spectinomycin (25 mg/kg intramuscularly, up to a maximum of 75 mg). Due to the significant benefits of treatment, neonates should be treated promptly, with the choice of medication depending on cost, quality, and local resistance patterns. The guidelines emphasize the importance of incorporating updated global recommendations into national protocols, adapting them to local epidemiological and antimicrobial susceptibility data. They also highlight the need for strengthened surveillance of antimicrobial resistance in N. gonorrhoeae and the development of rapid diagnostic tests to improve STI management. The prevention and control of STIs, including gonorrhea, are critical components of comprehensive sexual and reproductive health services, contributing to the achievement of universal health coverage and related Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).
